A year earlier the same queue held 1.9 GW. The report lists 31 data center requests and sorts them by how far each has travelled: 0.9 GW with signed interconnection agreements, 1.4 GW that has finished system impact studies, and 2.5 GW still waiting for a first study. Those studies, the authority says, now average 14 months, against 8 months in 2024.

My reading is that the headline number is the least useful figure in the report. The 4.8 GW measures demand for a place in line. The 0.9 GW measures load with a contract behind it. Everything a buyer, lender or operator has to decide in the next two years sits in the gap between those two numbers, and the report itself shows how slowly that gap will close. The source describes the queue and the limits of the wires. It says nothing about any project's construction status, so what follows about delivery timing is inference from queue data rather than from site evidence.

## A queued megawatt is an option

Filing a request costs a developer little and obliges the grid operator to study it. That is why queues grow faster than buildings do. In Northvale the queue more than doubled in a year, while the share with signed agreements stayed small. Less than a fifth of the 4.8 GW has an agreement, and more than half has not been studied at all.

The authority's own forecast treats the queue the same way. It expects peak demand on its system to rise 18 percent by 2031, yet it builds that forecast only on the 0.9 GW with signed agreements and calls everything else uncertain. When the operator responsible for the wires discounts most of its own queue, nobody buying capacity should count that queue at face value.

The readiness deposit points in the same direction. From 1 March 2027, a new request will have to post $50,000 per megawatt, refunded only once the project reaches commercial operation, and requests that cannot show site control will be dropped. The authority expects that rule to clear out some speculative filings. I read the deposit as the authority finally pricing an option that a queue position used to hand out for free.

A queued megawatt in Northvale is an option, and the authority has started to charge for it.

## Where the wires run out

The more binding figure is 1.1 GW. That is the additional load the authority says its transmission system can serve before 2029 without new substations or line upgrades. Set beside the 0.9 GW that already holds agreements, the headroom left for everyone else before 2029 looks thin. The report does not say how that 1.1 GW will be allocated, so the comparison is mine, and it is an inference about allocation rather than a reported fact.

Beyond that headroom, every project needs network upgrades, and the authority assigns their cost to the customers that ask for them. It puts those upgrades at $2.3 billion for the requests now queued. It does not say how the bill will be split among projects that share a substation. That missing rule decides whether any single project can be financed, because a lender cannot size a loan against an upgrade cost nobody has assigned.

The two largest campuses show the problem in concrete form. Together they account for 1.6 GW of the queue. Both are planned for AI training and inference, and both are seeking project financing. Neither has a signed agreement, and neither falls inside the 1.1 GW the authority can serve without upgrades. Anyone lending to either campus is lending against a connection that depends on upgrades with an unallocated cost and no published date.

Power before 2029 in Northvale is a question of contract position, and queue position barely enters into it.

## What a buyer should do with the queue

The decision rule I take from this report is my analysis, not something the authority recommends. For capacity that must be energized before 2029, count only megawatts with signed interconnection agreements. Treat studied but unsigned load as possible but unscheduled. Treat unstudied load as a signal of demand, never as supply.

For a hyperscale buyer, that rule changes which conversations matter. A developer holding a signed agreement holds something scarce and will price it accordingly. A developer with a large request and no study holds a place in a slow line, and a 14 month study means even a quick answer arrives long after a lease would have to be signed. Lease terms should follow the milestone that is actually evidenced, with rent and ready-for-service dates tied to the interconnection agreement rather than to the queue filing.

For lenders the rule is sharper still. The authority gives no energization date for any queued request, so a loan whose repayment assumes power on a given date is underwriting a date nobody has published.

Should they remove most speculative requests, studies could speed up and the line behind the signed projects could move faster than the 14 month average implies. The 18 percent growth the authority forecasts by 2031 also shows that it expects real load to arrive, and a grid operator that forecasts growth has a reason to approve upgrades. Approval and a quick allocation of the $2.3 billion of upgrades would turn the 1.1 GW ceiling into a near-term constraint rather than a structural one.

I weigh this less, for a reason the report itself supplies. The forecast that shows growth assumes that only the 0.9 GW with signed agreements gets built on schedule. Next is the queue report due in February 2027. json.title: In Northvale, signed load matters more than the 4.8 GW headline
json.deck: The Northvale Grid Authority's queue report shows 4.8 GW of data center requests but only 0.9 GW under signed agreements, so buyers should price queued megawatts as options rather than capacity.
json.thesis: Before 2029, only the 0.9 GW with signed agreements in Northvale should be treated as deliverable capacity, and buyers should price the rest of the queue as optional supply.
json.body:
Data center developers now want 4.8 GW of new load connected to the Northvale grid, according to the quarterly interconnection queue report the Northvale Grid Authority published on 12 November 2026. A year earlier the same queue held 1.9 GW. The report lists 31 data center requests and sorts them by how far each has travelled: 0.9 GW with signed interconnection agreements, 1.4 GW that has finished system impact studies, and 2.5 GW still waiting for a first study. Those studies, the authority says, now average 14 months, against 8 months in 2024.

My reading is that the headline number is the least useful figure in the report. The 4.8 GW measures demand for a place in line. The 0.9 GW measures load with a contract behind it. Everything a buyer, lender or operator has to decide in the next two years sits in the gap between those two numbers, and the report itself shows how slowly that gap will close. The source describes the queue and the limits of the wires. It says nothing about any project's construction status, so what follows about delivery timing is inference from queue data rather than from site evidence.

## A queued megawatt is an option

Filing a request costs a developer little and obliges the grid operator to study it. That is why queues grow faster than buildings do. In Northvale the queue more than doubled in a year, while the share with signed agreements stayed small. Less than a fifth of the 4.8 GW has an agreement, and more than half has not been studied at all.

The authority's own forecast treats the queue the same way. It expects peak demand on its system to rise 18 percent by 2031, yet it builds that forecast only on the 0.9 GW with signed agreements and calls everything else uncertain. When the operator responsible for the wires discounts most of its own queue, nobody buying capacity should count that queue at face value.

The readiness deposit points in the same direction. From 1 March 2027, a new request will have to post $50,000 per megawatt, refunded only once the project reaches commercial operation, and requests that cannot show site control will be dropped. The authority expects that rule to clear out some speculative filings. I read the deposit as the authority finally pricing an option that a queue position used to hand out for free.

A queued megawatt in Northvale is an option, and the authority has started to charge for it.

## Where the wires run out

The more binding figure is 1.1 GW. That is the additional load the authority says its transmission system can serve before 2029 without new substations or line upgrades. Set beside the 0.9 GW that already holds agreements, the headroom left for everyone else before 2029 looks thin. The report does not say how that 1.1 GW will be allocated, so the comparison is mine, and it is an inference about allocation rather than a reported fact.

Beyond that headroom, every project needs network upgrades, and the authority assigns their cost to the customers that ask for them. It puts those upgrades at $2.3 billion for the requests now queued. It does not say how the bill will be split among projects that share a substation. That missing rule decides whether any single project can be financed, because a lender cannot size a loan against an upgrade cost nobody has assigned.

The two largest campuses show the problem in concrete form. Together they account for 1.6 GW of the queue. Both are planned for AI training and inference, and both are seeking project financing. Neither has a signed agreement, and neither falls inside the 1.1 GW the authority can serve without upgrades. Anyone lending to either campus is lending against a connection that depends on upgrades with an unallocated cost and no published date.

Power before 2029 in Northvale is a question of contract position, and queue position barely enters into it.

## What a buyer should do with the queue

The decision rule I take from this report is my analysis, not something the authority recommends. For capacity that must be energized before 2029, count only megawatts with signed interconnection agreements. Treat studied but unsigned load as possible but unscheduled. Treat unstudied load as a signal of demand, never as supply.

For a hyperscale buyer, that rule changes which conversations matter. A developer holding a signed agreement holds something scarce and will price it accordingly. A developer with a large request and no study holds a place in a slow line, and a 14 month study means even a quick answer arrives long after a lease would have to be signed. Lease terms should follow the milestone that is actually evidenced, with rent and ready-for-service dates tied to the interconnection agreement rather than to the queue filing.

For lenders the rule is sharper still. The authority gives no energization date for any queued request, so a loan whose repayment assumes power on a given date is underwriting a date nobody has published.

Underwrite the agreement, not the request.
json.counterpoint:
## The case that the queue clears faster than it looks

There is a credible argument that this reading is too cautious. The readiness deposit and the site-control rule exist to shrink the queue. Should they remove most speculative requests, studies could speed up and the line behind the signed projects could move faster than the 14 month average implies. The 18 percent growth the authority forecasts by 2031 also shows that it expects real load to arrive, and a grid operator that forecasts growth has a reason to approve upgrades. Approval and a quick allocation of the $2.3 billion of upgrades would turn the 1.1 GW ceiling into a near-term constraint rather than a structural one.

I weigh this less, for a reason the report itself supplies. The forecast that shows growth assumes that only the 0.9 GW with signed agreements gets built on schedule. The authority is not counting on the rest of its queue, and a buyer should not either, at least until a deposit has been posted, a study finished and an agreement signed. The argument does narrow my thesis. A deposit that clears the queue quickly would give the studied 1.4 GW a better chance than unstudied load, and that difference belongs in the price.
json.implications:
## Three filings that will settle the timeline

First comes the stakeholder meeting on the readiness deposit in January 2027. A deposit that survives at $50,000 per megawatt, refunded only at commercial operation, would likely shrink the queue and leave more serious requests behind; a diluted or delayed deposit would leave the 4.8 GW overstating demand for another cycle.

Next is the queue report due in February 2027. Growth in the signed share beyond 0.9 GW, with fewer megawatts waiting for a first study, would mean the line is moving and studied projects can be priced closer to firm capacity. Growth in the 2.5 GW that has never been studied would mean the study backlog is the real constraint, and every delivery date should move out.

Last is any decision on how the $2.3 billion of network upgrades is divided among projects that share a substation. Clear project-by-project shares would let the two large campuses raise money on known terms. An open allocation would leave neither with a bankable connection. The report gives no date for that decision, and the absence of one is itself the thing to watch.
